questions.question: Who was the first king of Israel?
questions.explanation: King Saul was the first king of Israel. King David established and consolidated the kingdom.

questions.question: Who built the first Jewish Temple?
questions.explanation: King Solomon built the first Jewish Temple in Jerusalem.

questions.question: When and by whom was the Northern Kingdom conquered?
questions.explanation: The Northern Kingdom fell in 722 BC to the Assyrians under Sargon II.

questions.question: What are the people taken from the Northern tribes into captivity called?
questions.explanation: They are called the Lost Ten Tribes — they were never recorded as returning.

questions.question: When and by whom was the Southern Kingdom conquered?
questions.explanation: 586 BC by Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon. Jews returned to Jerusalem around 538 BC and built the Second Temple.

questions.question: What is Hellenism?
options: The mass-appeal popular culture of antiquity spread by Greek influence
questions.explanation: Hellenism was the mass-appeal popular culture of antiquity. Greek became the lingua franca; Near Eastern art adopted Greco-style forms; many regions adopted Greek gods under new names.

questions.question: Who was responsible for spreading Greek culture throughout the world?
questions.explanation: Alexander the Great spread Greek culture (Hellenism) throughout the known world.

questions.question: Which empire ruled Judea during Jesus's lifetime?
questions.explanation: Rome ruled Judea from 63 BC onward. Jesus lived approximately 4 BC – 30 AD.

questions.question: Who was Herod the Great?
options: A Jewish high priest appointed by the Pharisees
A Roman Emperor who conquered Judea
An Idumean king appointed by Rome who expanded the Second Temple
A Hasmonean prince who revolted against Rome
questions.explanation: Herod the Great was appointed by the Romans, reigned 37 BC–4 AD, was an Idumean convert who married a Hasmonean princess, expanded the Second Temple, and is known for the Massacre of the Infants.

questions.question: Which Herod was responsible for beheading John the Baptist?
questions.explanation: Herod Antipas was the tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, and was responsible for beheading John the Baptist.

questions.question: What are the scriptural passages that support the Israelite conception of a Messiah? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Deuteronomy 18:15, 2 Samuel 7:12,13,16, and Daniel 7:13 are the key passages. The Messiah was conceived as a king and military-political leader, not primarily a redeemer from sin.

questions.question: Why is it inaccurate to speak of 'Judaism' (singular) at the time of Jesus?
options: Judaism had not yet developed as a religion
There were multiple types of Judaism — Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes, Zealots, etc.
Most Jews had converted to Hellenism
questions.explanation: There were multiple distinct Jewish sects and movements at the time, including Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes, and Zealots — each with different beliefs and practices.

questions.question: What were the three elements of Jewish orthodoxy (correct belief)? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The three elements were: Monotheism (one God), Election (chosen people), and Eschatology (hope for a future day of restoration).

questions.question: What were the three elements of Jewish orthopraxy (correct practice)? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The three elements were: Temple (center of sacrifice), Torah (law), and Priesthood (mediated the temple cult).

questions.question: Which Jewish group built a 'hedge' around the Law and was associated with synagogues?
questions.explanation: The Pharisees were known for their strict interpretation of the Torah AND oral traditions (Oral Law). They were law scholars associated with synagogues who built a 'hedge' around the law.

questions.question: Which Jewish group denied the resurrection of the dead?
questions.explanation: The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy. They accepted only the written Torah and Prophets, which led them to deny the resurrection.

questions.question: What texts were the Essenes responsible for?
questions.explanation: The Essenes were an ascetic desert sect who acted as scribes and produced the Dead Sea Scrolls. They saw themselves as 'Sons of Light' and were focused on messianic texts.

questions.question: Why are the Dead Sea Scrolls important?
options: They are the original autographs of the New Testament
They contain the oldest known manuscript excerpts of the Hebrew Bible and illuminate Judaism's diversity
They prove Jesus was an Essene
They are the original source of the Torah
questions.explanation: The Dead Sea Scrolls are the oldest known manuscript excerpts of the Hebrew Bible (including Isaiah, Daniel, and the Book of Enoch), illuminating the religious environment and Judaism's diversity.

questions.question: How were Samaritans similar to Jews? (Select all that apply)
options: Used the same Temple in Jerusalem
questions.explanation: Samaritans were monotheistic, believed in a Messiah, and claimed to be Jewish. However, they had mixed blood, their own temple, and their own Torah — and rejected other Jewish scripture.

questions.question: When and by whom was Jerusalem destroyed (Second Temple)?
questions.explanation: 70 AD by Roman General Titus. This triggered the second Jewish Diaspora and shifted Judaism from temple-centered to synagogue-centered (rabbinic Judaism).

questions.question: What were the three requirements to become a Jew? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The three requirements were Ritual Purification, Circumcision, and Living the Law of Moses.

questions.question: What does 'Soteriology' mean?
options: The study of last things and afterlife
The study of the Jewish Diaspora
The study of Christ's role as Savior — how Jesus saves humanity
questions.explanation: 'Soter' means savior. Soteriology is specifically a Christian theological concept — the study of Christ's role as Savior.

questions.question: What is Sheol?
options: The Jewish concept of Hell, a place of punishment
The Jewish concept of the underworld/spirit world, where people are reunited with ancestors
questions.explanation: Sheol is the Jewish concept of the underworld/spirit world. After death, people go to Sheol and are reunited with ancestors — it is not a fully developed heaven/hell scheme.

questions.question: What language did Jesus and his followers speak?
questions.explanation: Jesus and his followers spoke Aramaic, the common language of the region.

questions.question: What language was the New Testament originally written in?
questions.explanation: The New Testament was originally written in Greek.

questions.question: How many original manuscripts (autographs) of the New Testament still exist?
questions.explanation: No original manuscripts (autographs) of the New Testament still exist.

questions.question: What is the Vulgate and who produced it?
options: A Greek manuscript collection by Origen
A Latin translation of the Bible by Jerome
The first English Bible by Wycliffe
questions.explanation: The Vulgate is a Latin translation of the Bible produced by Jerome.

questions.question: What process is most responsible for the majority of errors in New Testament manuscripts?
questions.explanation: Transmission — the process of copying manuscripts by hand — is responsible for the majority of errors in the New Testament manuscripts.

questions.question: What was the first Bible printed in English?
questions.explanation: The Wycliffe Bible (1382) was the first Bible printed in English.

questions.question: Why is the Tyndale Bible so important?
options: It was the first English Bible and was commissioned by a king
It was the first English translation directly from the original Greek, and the KJV is based on it
It was the first Bible with chapter and verse numbers
It was the first Catholic English translation
questions.explanation: The Tyndale Bible was the first English translation directly from the original Greek. The King James Version is largely based on Tyndale's work.

questions.question: When was the King James Bible printed, and why was it commissioned?
options: 1382, to create the first English Bible
1611, commissioned in 1604 by King James I to stop the Protestant trend
questions.explanation: The King James Bible was printed in 1611, commissioned in 1604 by King James I to produce a definitive translation and stop the Protestant trend.

questions.question: What is the Apocrypha?
options: Lost books of the Old Testament discovered recently
Books included in the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox canons but not Protestant, meaning 'of doubtful origin'
The oral traditions of the Pharisees
questions.explanation: The Apocrypha literally means 'of doubtful origin.' These books are canonical for Catholics and Eastern Orthodox Christians, but not Protestants. They provide valuable insight into the faith of that era.

questions.question: Who provided the first list of 27 New Testament books matching our current canon?
questions.explanation: Bishop Athanasius of Alexandria in 367 AD provided the first list of the 27 New Testament books that matches our current canon.

questions.question: What is Exegesis vs. Eisegesis?
options: Exegesis = original meaning; Eisegesis = modern application
Exegesis = literal reading; Eisegesis = symbolic reading
Exegesis = Jewish interpretation; Eisegesis = Christian interpretation
Exegesis = what they meant; Eisegesis = what it means to me
questions.explanation: Exegesis means drawing out what the author originally meant. Eisegesis means reading one's own meaning into the text.

questions.question: Who is Luke? What was his background and occupation?
options: A Pharisee and lawyer from Jerusalem
questions.explanation: Luke was a Gentile physician from Antioch. He wrote the Gospel of Luke and the Book of Acts, and his Greek is the most sophisticated in the New Testament.

questions.question: What are the four themes of the Book of Acts? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The four themes are: (1) Geographic spread of the Gospel, (2) Jewish to Jew + Gentile inclusion, (3) Role of the Holy Ghost, and (4) Defense of Christianity.

questions.question: To whom is the Book of Acts addressed?
questions.explanation: The Book of Acts is addressed to Theophilus (as is the Gospel of Luke).

questions.question: What does 'passion' mean in a New Testament context?
options: The suffering and Atonement of Jesus
questions.explanation: In NT context, 'passion' refers to the suffering and Atonement of Jesus.

questions.question: What happened during Jesus's forty-day ministry after the resurrection?
options: Jesus relayed sacred teachings (gnosis) between His resurrection and Ascension
Jesus appeared to over 500 people in the marketplace
Jesus dictated scripture to the apostles
questions.explanation: During the forty-day ministry, Jesus relayed sacred teachings (gnosis) between His resurrection and Ascension.

questions.question: Who replaced Judas Iscariot as a member of the Twelve?
questions.explanation: Matthias was chosen to replace Judas Iscariot.

questions.question: What is the Day of Pentecost?
options: 50 days after Passover, first fruits harvest, to remember Noah's covenant; now associated with the miraculous manifestation of the Holy Spirit
The day Jesus ascended into heaven
questions.explanation: Pentecost is 50 days after Passover, originally a first fruits harvest celebration to remember Noah's covenant. It is now associated with the miraculous manifestation of the Holy Spirit described in Acts 2.

questions.question: What are the four parts of the Pentecostal package (as described by Peter in Acts 2)? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The four parts are: Repentance, Baptism, Gift of the Holy Ghost, and Enduring to the End. Peter does NOT explicitly mention faith in this passage.

questions.question: Who was Barnabas?
options: A Roman centurion who became a disciple
A Levite from Cyprus who sold a field and gave proceeds to the apostles
One of the original Twelve Apostles
questions.explanation: Barnabas was a Levite from Cyprus who sold a field and gave the proceeds to the apostles (Acts 4).

questions.question: What was the sin of Ananias and Sapphira?
options: Lying to the Holy Spirit about their donation while secretly keeping some back
questions.explanation: Their sin was lying to the Holy Spirit about their donation — they claimed to give all the proceeds from their land sale but secretly kept some back (Acts 5).

questions.question: Who was Stephen?
options: A Roman soldier who converted to Christianity
A Hellenist charged with blasphemy who became Christianity's first martyr
One of the original Twelve Apostles
questions.explanation: Stephen was a Hellenist charged with blasphemy and speaking against the Law and the Temple. He was stoned after his speech, becoming the first Christian martyr.

questions.question: Who held the clothes of those who stoned Stephen?
questions.explanation: Saul (later Paul) held the clothes of those who stoned Stephen (Acts 7:58).

questions.question: What is the significance of the Ethiopian eunuch (Acts 8)?
options: He was the first Gentile to receive the Holy Spirit
He crossed ethnic and physical inclusion boundaries — not circumcised, but a God-fearing person
He was a Roman soldier who believed in Jesus
He translated the scriptures into Amharic
questions.explanation: The Ethiopian eunuch was a God-fearing person who was not circumcised. His baptism expanded the church's boundaries by crossing ethnic and physical lines.

questions.question: Who was Cornelius and why is he significant?
options: A Jewish high priest who believed in Jesus
A Roman Centurion and God-fearer who was baptized while uncircumcised
A Greek philosopher who converted to Christianity
A Samaritan leader who hosted the apostles
questions.explanation: Cornelius was a Roman Centurion and God-fearer who was wealthy. He was baptized while uncircumcised, marking a key expansion of the church to Gentiles.

questions.question: What was the significance of Peter's vision in Acts 10 (the sheet with animals)?
options: It revealed that Peter would travel to Rome
It challenged dietary restrictions and redefined the church's boundaries — an 'Abrahamic test'
It predicted the destruction of the Temple
It confirmed that the Sabbath was no longer required
questions.explanation: Peter's vision challenged dietary restrictions and boundaries of table fellowship. It served as an 'Abrahamic test' and redefined the church's boundaries to include Gentiles.

questions.question: What were the four cultural markers of Judaism? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The four cultural markers were: Circumcision, Sabbath Observance, Purity Regulations, and Dietary Restrictions.

questions.question: What were the earliest followers of Jesus called?
questions.explanation: The earliest followers of Jesus were called 'Followers of the Way.'

questions.question: How was Paul a citizen of three worlds? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Paul was a citizen of three worlds: Jewish by religion, Greek by culture, and Roman by citizenship.

questions.question: Which Jewish party did Paul most closely align with?
questions.explanation: Paul was a Pharisee before his conversion.

questions.question: What is the significance of the shift from 'Saul' to 'Paul'?
options: Paul received a new name from God at his conversion
Paul was his Roman/Greek nickname meaning 'little dog'; not a new name — he used it as he went to the Gentiles
Paul changed his name to distance himself from his Jewish identity
The apostles gave him the name Paul after his baptism
questions.explanation: Paul was his Roman/Greek nickname, meaning 'little dog.' It was not a new name given at conversion — he simply used it more as he ministered to Gentiles.

questions.question: What was Saul's occupation prior to his vision of Jesus?
questions.explanation: Saul was a tentmaker or leatherworker before (and during) his ministry.

questions.question: Who served as Paul's first missionary companion?
questions.explanation: Barnabas served as Paul's first missionary companion.

questions.question: What happened to Mark (John Mark) on Paul's first mission?
options: He was a young man who left the mission; later he was with Peter, wrote a gospel, and founded the church at Alexandria
He became Paul's main disciple and replaced Barnabas
He stayed in Antioch as leader of the church there
questions.explanation: Mark (a relative of Barnabas) left the first mission early. He later worked with Peter, wrote the Gospel of Mark, and is credited with founding the church at Alexandria.

questions.question: Where did Paul go on his first missionary journey (47–48 AD)?
options: Perga, Antioch, Iconium, Lystra — centered in Antioch
questions.explanation: Paul's first missionary journey (47–48 AD) covered Perga, Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra, with the center in Antioch.

questions.question: What are the four parts of a Pauline epistle? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The four parts are: Opening, Thanksgiving, Main Body (Indicative + Imperative), and Closing (Signature of sender).

questions.question: What is the core problem in Galatia that Paul addresses in his letter?
options: Circumcision being required; Judaizers claiming Paul is inferior and not a true apostle
questions.explanation: Paul addresses the circumcision issue — Judaizers were claiming that Gentile converts must be circumcised and that Paul's authority was inferior to the Jerusalem apostles.

questions.question: What does Paul mean by calling himself an 'apostle' in Galatians 1:1?
options: He is claiming to be equal to Peter and James
He claims divine authority directly from the risen Christ, not from human appointment
He is using the term loosely to mean a traveling missionary
He received his authority from the church in Antioch
questions.explanation: Paul uses 'apostle' (one sent) to claim direct divine authority from the risen Christ, not from human appointment — legitimizing his mission to the Gentiles.

questions.question: What term do scholars use for Paul's opponents in Galatia?
questions.explanation: Paul's opponents are called Judaizers — Jewish Christians who insisted Gentiles must follow Torah (especially circumcision) to be saved.

questions.question: Why did Paul have a dispute with Peter (Galatians 2)?
options: Peter denied Jesus for a second time publicly
Peter stopped eating with Gentile believers after Jewish men from James arrived, which Paul called hypocrisy
Peter taught that circumcision was unnecessary even for Jews
questions.explanation: Peter stopped eating with Gentile believers after 'certain men from James' arrived, fearing criticism from the circumcision party. Paul rebuked this publicly as hypocrisy.

questions.question: What does Paul mean by 'faith' (pistis)?
options: Allegiance and loyalty; trust in Christ
The spiritual gift of miraculous belief
questions.explanation: For Paul, pistis means allegiance/loyalty — trust and faithfulness to Christ.

questions.question: What does Paul mean by 'works' in Galatians?
options: Works of the Law of Moses (Torah observance)
questions.explanation: For Paul, 'works' specifically means 'works of the Law' — Torah observance as a requirement for covenant membership.

questions.question: What does 'justification' mean for Paul?
options: Being declared not guilty; covenant membership/righteousness in Christ
The process of becoming holy over time
The act of confessing one's sins
questions.explanation: Justification means being declared not guilty; it refers to covenant membership and righteousness in Christ.

questions.question: Who is James at the Council of Jerusalem?
options: James the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve
The brother of Jesus, leader of the Jerusalem church, important at the Council
A Pharisee who converted after the resurrection
The author of the Epistle of James who wrote from Rome
questions.explanation: James the brother of Jesus was the leader of the Jerusalem church and played a key role at the Council of Jerusalem.

questions.question: What was the verdict at the Council of Jerusalem?
options: All Gentile converts must be circumcised and follow the Law of Moses
Gentile converts do not need circumcision; they should abstain from idol food, sexual immorality, strangled animals, and blood
The church would split into Jewish and Gentile branches
questions.explanation: The Council decided Gentiles did not need to be circumcised or keep the whole Law. They were asked to abstain from: (1) food polluted by idols, (2) sexual immorality, (3) meat of strangled animals, and (4) blood.

questions.question: Why did Paul and Barnabas part ways?
options: They disagreed about whether to preach to Gentiles
They fought over John Mark — Barnabas wanted to take him; Paul disagreed. Barnabas took Mark to Cyprus; Paul took Silas.
Paul was arrested and Barnabas left the mission
They had a theological disagreement about circumcision
questions.explanation: Paul and Barnabas parted ways before the second missionary journey over John Mark. Barnabas took Mark to Cyprus; Paul took Silas.
